utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Higgins.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before Mr. Nice begins his cross-examination, can I just clarify in relation to the five documents that were shown to General Jelic by Mr. Milosevic towards the end of yesterday, four of them have been previously admitted through the testimony of General Delic. One has not been, and it might be thought prudent in analysing the testimony of this witness that the five short documents are readmitted as a subtab, and the liaison office is preparing copies for the Chamber and the parties this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you just identify the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. HIGGINS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first document, which was dated the 2nd of March, 1999, was Delic D300, tab 449. The second document, which was the only document not previously admitted, was in fact dated the 29th of the 10th, 1998, and it was originally D300, tab 166, but not admitted through Delic. The third document, which was admitted through Delic, dated the 3rd of March, 1999, was D300, tab 450. The fourth document was D300, tab 456, and it's difficult for me to see the date. I think it's the 8th of the 3rd, 1999. And the fifth document, dated the 4th of January, 1999, was previously D300, tab 265, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Higgins. In the third and final session of tomorrow's hearing, the Chamber will hear submissions on the question of extension of the time allocated to the accused for the presentation of his Defence. Each party will be allowed 15 minutes. Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, did you serve in the Croatian conflict?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you serve in the Bosnian conflict?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you based in the period of time 1991 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Nis garrison. I was the commander of the police and the commander of a Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with staffing or providing forces for the Serb side in either the Croatian conflict or the Bosnian conflict?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. I was a brigade commander, holding the border towards Republic of Bulgaria.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your troops ever go and fight in Croatia or in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of my troops except for those who ended their term of military service and went to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you understand in the course of 1992, 1993, 1994 or 1995 how it was that Serb troops were sent to fight in the Krajina or in the Republika Srpska? Did you understand how that was done?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a single unit of mine went to the Republic of Croatia or to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The units that did go went under orders from the superior command. Those were neighbouring units who gave part of their troops within the scope of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the method by which it was done, sending troops within the scope of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever units are sent somewhere to carry out an assignment, whether inside or outside their area of responsibility, it's done pursuant to an order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but what was the actual mechanism? Did you understand whether troops were sent frankly, candidly, openly and honestly to serve for the RS or were they sent to some fictional destination?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that because nobody from my units went there. As for other units, I know they went in compliance with orders. I was not familiar with the content of the orders. I had some information about it, but I was not fully informed. I was in Nis up to 1994. In 1994, I was at the Urosevac garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where were you in July 1994?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1994, I was in Urosevac; from May onwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were now with the 243rd already, were you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 243rd Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We've heard something called -- we've heard evidence about things called the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres. Do you know anything about them?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that this personnel centre existed, but I did not have access to those documents or orders, and I was not fully informed about its functioning. My unit was not covered by those orders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. You had no dealings with the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre, which took Serb soldiers to fight in Croatia or in Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never had any dealings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... take a look at this, please. I'm afraid it's only in B/C/S and we haven't got copies at the moment, but if we can lay it on the overhead projector. Perhaps you would like to look at the second page first. Bottom of the page, please, Mr. Prendergast, so we can see the signature and everything. This appears to come from you in 1994 in your role as commander of the 243rd. If we go back to the first page now, please, Mr. Prendergast. Can you just read out the first paragraph, please. You can see the date. Just read out for us starting from --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The 27th of July, 1994. Urgent."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you please read more slowly for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "From the 26th of July, 1994, we hereby submit the requested information, a list of officers of Serbian and Montenegrin nationality who were born or sent for schooling or admitted for military service from the territory of the Republic of Croatia and the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. 30th Personnel Centre. Jovan Tomic, son of Simo, Serb captain."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... see another list of the 40th Personnel Centre. So it appears you did know about the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres in 1994. Yes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just let me have a look. I did know that the centres existed. None of these officers in the period while I was brigade commander was in Bosnia and Herzegovina or in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... marked under the 30th or 40th Personnel Centres. What were they doing, sitting in Belgrade in an office headed 30th or 40th Personnel Centre? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at the conversations they had. I was the garrison command. I did not leave the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. These officers went to attend meetings and this was one of those meetings. However, not a single one of those officers went either to Croatia or to Bosnia and Herzegovina. Up to the 16th of June, 1999, they remained in my brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're here clearly identifying officers under the heading 30th or 40th Personnel Centre. You've now referred to a discussion. What was it all about? Did officers who were born in particular places go and have meetings together or something?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are persons who were born in the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what were they doing in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres? Please help us.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that they joined the army from the territory of the Republics of Croatia or Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where they joined the army. And they originate from Bosnia and Herzegovina or Croatia, and -- they originated from those areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you can't explain the heading 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask for the document to be exhibited, marked for identification pending a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI 932.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, we've been looking at the map on the board behind you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would a copy of the document please be given to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Everybody will have a copy as soon as I've got them brought downstairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that is to be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jelic, the map behind you has got markings on it, and there's no suggestion that the Bench or I or anybody else in this court has military expertise, so we mustn't assume that we do. Who drew this map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps decision on -- decisions on the use of the brigade are made by the corps commander. This was most probably drawn up by the operations organ of the Pristina Corps. It says here that this is an excerpt for the 243rd Mechanised Brigade. These are documents for subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the entire map that is delivered to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that exhibit so that we don't lose track of what you're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 1 of this witness's exhibits, which are Defence exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll get the Defence exhibit number but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 329, but from now on I'll just use tab numbers. 329, tab 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was it drawn, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map was drawn just before the aggression against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That's what you say. Where did this particular document come from?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document is from the command of the Pristina Corps, the commander, and it's sent to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This particular document that the accused has produced through you and is now on the easel, where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The collaborators of the accused showed it to me in the tabs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at another exhibit which is an existing exhibit, Exhibit 319, tab 62, which has been -- just on the overhead projector will do, I think -- which has been highlighted, just to see if you agree with what I'm going to suggest to you, and it may help matters. In general terms, if we look at this map, do we see -- thank you very much, that's fine. Do we see the four parts of Kosovo at the material time, divided up as between the 549th Brigade on the south-west; your brigade, the 243rd, on the south-east; the 125th on the north-west; and then the 150th on the north-east? 15th, I beg your pardon, on the north-east. Is that division of the territory as between those four units roughly correct? We're going to come to precision later so I just want, in order to help the Court, to see if you accept that that is roughly correct.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is roughly correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, the Pristina Corps is in charge of one, two, three, or four of those sectors?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps commands all the brigades, not sectors. All the brigades listed here are subordinated to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back, please, to the map tab 1. Can we look at tab 1 now, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution, the 319.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Must be -- I think you're mistaken with the number. 319.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did I say 319?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you check it out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Nice, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've established in general terms and reminded the Chamber what this is, now please look at the map on the easel. You say this is an extract and you say this was, what, prepared in 1999? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. The army commander then was General Samardzic. As you can see, it's not the same signature on this map where it says "I approve." This is the original map, the one on the board there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. When was this map produced?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map was produced in March, just before the aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was produced by the Pristina Corps you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the little map we've looked at that the Pristina Corps covered your area of operation, Delic's area of operation, the 125th and the 15th. Now if you'd look at what you say is an extract from this map can you explain to us, please, why there are no military markings to the west of the markings that relate to your unit, your brigade. Take the pointer, please. Point to the figure of the 549th. Now, to the west of that there is no military marking. So if what you're telling us is true and this is the extract of a Pristina Corps map, it's rather curious because it hasn't marked what it should have been marking for Delic's area of operation. Can you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Every brigade or every subordinate unit, when it is given an assignment by the subordinate command, receives its assignment in detail. The neighbouring units to the left and to the right, in front or behind, their tasks are entered only in principle, only roughly, and the same goes for written orders as well as for maps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for some reason you're provided with information that doesn't include what's happening in the adjoining territory.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see, only the neighbouring unit next to the brigade is entered, and the brigade is entered as a whole.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, what does this map show us, please? Tell us. What does it show?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the initial disposition of the brigade before the aggression. The brigade carried out full mobilisation. It took up its positions, fortified them, and took all security measures to protect the state border, that is the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, to protect the men and the equipment, bearing in mind that at the border terrorist forces were building up in a strength of five brigades and NATO forces, one Mechanised Brigade, two Armoured Brigades --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was the map marked subsequently or is what we've got a map frozen in time at a date mid-March 1999?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This map covers the period in the end of March 1999. This is the initial disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You understand my question? It's frozen in time. It doesn't reflect things that happened after the initial disposition.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand. How can you say frozen in time? This is the deployment of the units. Could you please rephrase your question. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're not military men here. You have to help us. People may have seen, either in entertainment films or in documentaries, military people taking maps and marking them with events as events unfold. Is this a map which has been marked with events as they unfolded, with changes of disposition of troops, with local battles, whatever it might be, or is it a map frozen in time; this is the initial disposition of troops?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, just as you put it. This map shows the initial disposition of the troops, especially for blocking defence. The other thing is completely different. That is a working map following developments in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And somewhere the working map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the working map here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, where is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- well, like all documents, they were handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they still exist somewhere but they haven't been brought to court, yes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say because parts of commands were destroyed, like my own, so I really cannot answer that question whether it still exists or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you looked at those maps?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was transferred to be head of the higher military academy when I left the Pristina Corps, I practically had no further access to the unit where I was before, and nobody asked me to do that, to seek these documents, and I don't think that would be my obligation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a second. Mr. Prendergast, if you would be so good. Could you lay on the overhead projector this copy of tab 1. There are three places I've marked with stickers so that we can -- there's no legend. I've been -- no explanation of the entries on it and therefore I'm going to have to try to find out what this map means if you're going to refer to it. So if you just look at three entries on this map. The ones on -- that's fine as it is at the moment. And if you could focus in on the two yellow stickers. Thank you very much. You'll see these little entries here. One is at Kacanik to the north and is a black oval filled with yellow. What does that mean? Put a sticker by it with an arrow. What does that circle or oval mean? Down a bit. There it is. What does that oval mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were the envisaged areas where chemical weapons could be used. Most probably you see that it is in the blue disposition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please -- remember, we're not military men. You've been pointing at this map without the advantage of a legend, with no explanation. It's your map. You tell us, what does that oval mean? Very simple. And if you can't explain it to us, that's fine. We'll then forget all about it.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably this is the area where the NATO forces or, rather, the units carrying out the aggression used chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That can't be --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how these areas are marked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That can't be right because you've told us this is a map frozen in time with initial dispositions. Now, you're a general. This is your map.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you understand the map or not?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't, we'll throw it away, metaphorically speaking. Do you understand this map?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand it perfectly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... General, tell us, please, what this map, created before the aggression, as you describe it, in March 1999 means by the black oval with the yellow filling. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These ovals, I've already said that. These are most probably the regions where the potential aggressor would be likely to use chemical weapons. Now, you say that this map was frozen in time. Can you see the blue, the aggressor, being marked even in-depth in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija? NATO forces never reached that area and the terrorists from Albania never reached that area either, but this shows probably what their likely action would be in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have your answer. South-east of that you'll see another little sticker - perhaps you'd like to point to it to make sure you understand where we're getting to - which is a little, small, round thing. There it is. That one. So what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just compare the two. It's most probably this one here. That is the PVO system, the anti-aircraft system, air defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That means that an anti-air system is going to be installed there or located there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Prendergast -- Mr. Prendergast --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- last of the three stickers. Now we've put this one here for two reasons. Is this area definitely within your area of operation? It's slightly to the west of Slapuzane.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This, right?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where the arrow is. That is an anti-armour detachment of the 549th Brigade, its reserve position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that although this is in part -- I beg your pardon. Although this shows your brigade's disposition, perhaps, as we suspected, this is something that is not part of the 243rd.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It's not part of the 243rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the symbol means what? You've mentioned it but I just want -- it's anti-armour detachment, is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anti-armour detachment. That is to say equipment that is envisaged for anti-armour combat. That is the symbol for that area. It is oval shaped, and it's coloured black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And also it is written here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's just -- thank you. Can I have that map back, please, Mr. Prendergast. Can we share another document that is in the process of preparation but until we had your answers we weren't quite sure. It doesn't need to be given an exhibit number at the moment or even -- doesn't become a candidate for an exhibit number at the moment. I just want to check certain things, if you'd like. If the audiovisual booth could come back. This is a map that's in preparation, Mr. Jelic, seeking to identify material locations and events within your area of responsibility. You'll see that the possible extent of your area of responsibility has been marked with locations inside it, but you'll see if you look at the west that there have been a number of places of some uncertainty that we just want to be sure don't relate to you. So if, for example, we start at the bottom: Geljance, Grejkovce, Djinovce, Trnje, Vranic, Budakovo, Bukos. Is any of those in your area of responsibility for do they all belong to Delic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you see here on the left-hand side are for the most part Jezerska Planina, and it is the 549th Motorised Brigade, its area of responsibility, although we don't have strict boundaries, so his zone and my zone overlap considerably. Suva Reka, though, is in his area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, then. Please look at those places. Perhaps -- you start at Papaz and work your way down: Papaz, Bukos, Budakovo, Vranic, and so on. Are there any of those place names that are place names where your brigade functioned and in respect of which you should have knowledge? If so, tell us with ones.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papaz is in my area of responsibility. Budakovo is not, Vranic is not, Trnje is not. Djinovce is not, Grejkovce is not -- is in my area of responsibility, and that is on the road to Strpce or Stimlje, on the border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and then I think that leaves Geljance and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose area of responsibility --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of that is in the area of responsibility of the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. To the north we can see north -- top left-hand side of the map we can see Belanica. Is that something over which you have authority and should have knowledge or does that belong to the next-door brigade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belanica was in front of the units at Dulje, Belince also, Racak in my area of responsibility, Jezerce, that's the boundary --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and Banjica and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- these other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just look at the east. We've seen places like Gnjilane, Vladovo, Zegra, Vitina, Drobes, Ljubiste. Is any of those an area over which you had responsibility and for which you should have knowledge? And finally, Smira. Any of those areas over which you had responsibility and over which you should have knowledge? If so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never commanded that because that was under the command of the 175th Brigade, which is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we get that map back, please. We'll get it prepared to reflect what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear the end of that sentence. General, would you repeat the answer. The interpreter did not hear the end of your sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Because the general was facing the map and not speaking into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These places you identified or, rather, that I showed here are in the municipality of Vitina and Gnjilane. They were not under my command. They were under the command of the 175th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you approached by the VJ Commission for Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you made no --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What commission do you mean? For cooperation? I don't understand. VJ Commission for Cooperation?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: VJ Commission for Cooperation presided over by Terzic, I think. It's been dealing with the evidence from military officers. Did it have contact with you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not establish contact with me. They did not address me in any way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You made no statements for them?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made no statements to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of their existence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Already in 2002 I retired. Nobody called me. I heard people talking about the existence of that commission. However, since I do not live in Belgrade, since I live in Nis, I could not have contact with them or, rather, nobody contacted me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- you told us yesterday of your war diary. Where is your war diary?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned this in one of these reports. All my documents, according to the decision of the corps commander, were handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps at the Pristina garrison. As for what happened later, I do not know. I don't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you mentioned this "in one of these reports." Which report are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report that went to the corps command. That's what it said in a telegram, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But these are the usual kind of documents that are kept at brigade level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that every officer from the rank -- or every unit from the rank of battalion up in time of war has to keep a war diary. So all the battalions answering to you kept war diaries.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Every battalion level unit has a war diary, keeps a war diary, but in war, once a state of war is declared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So from the end of -- of March 1999 at the latest, as well as your war diary, there are all the battalion diaries in existence, so far as you know, and stored in an archive?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that it was handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps. I don't know of their fate after that. The command was partly destroyed, just like my command. I cannot really say anything about how much is left, whether anything is left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, why do people keep war diaries?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is one of the basic documents. In addition to the order that is written in the text part as a basic document, and the maps, the decision is then depicted on a map and then this is a document where important events are recorded at units which are at the level of a battalion and higher up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But why keep one? Because it enables you to know what happened? Would that be roughly right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A diary is kept -- I mean, the word itself is linked to the word "day," so it records daily events that are relevant. It's a document that has a particular form, a way in which it is kept. The essence is that the most important things that happen during the course of a day are recorded there, as well as orders issued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that if you ever need to know what happened, you go to the diary. That's why you have a diary.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is kept in the operative organs, and if an order came a day earlier, then you turn the page, you look at the order, you see whether it was carried through. If not, it is then carried through and then the superior command is informed about this. So the point is that it records everything the brigade does, but it mainly relates to combat activities, not mere correspondence, mail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness before you, a man called Sel, who was a captain promoted to major in charge of a company, kept a personal diary and he made -- gave evidence - we are going to hear more about this - that he'd need such a document if there was ever any, I think, court issues involved, if he ever had to give evidence, or something like that. Did company commanders keep diaries or notebooks as a matter of routine or regulation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the microphone please be adjusted. The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the microphones be adjusted. The interpreters cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. This is an incredible assertion. Major Sel never said during his testimony that a war diary is kept if something is supposed to be discussed before a court of law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He said something about it and we have to discover what he said, but I want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did he actually say that, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I haven't got exact quote, but I want -- I still want to know from this witness, not from the accused, if I may say so, what the position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, but if you are quoting the evidence, then you must do so accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As far as I know I am. I'll try and find it for you. But -- perhaps Ms. Dicklich can do that for me. May I ask the witness a question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead. We'll come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, come back to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do company commanders keep contemporaneous diaries of one kind or another for whatever purpose?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Company commanders keep work notebooks. That is the lowest ranking officer who can write orders, but not necessarily. Company commanders; that's them. A work notebook, which is verified with a list of soldiers and all information about the unit, that is kept in that company. A war diary, though, is kept by the commander of the battalion or of the artillery battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with just the company commander level, again his notebook, it's not a personal choice whether he keeps such a notebook; he has to keep such a notebook. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are two types of work notebooks: A work notebook that includes all elements for the unit, that is to say the list of personnel, the list of equipment, and that is an official work notebook. Then there is a notebook because he doesn't work in the office, because he is out in the terrain, in the woods, under a tent, on a truck, then he takes notes regarding the orders he receives in that notebook. So then he personally uses it as an aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he -- but he is obliged, either by regulation, by rule, or by practice of the army, he is obliged to keep such a diary or notebook, whatever we call it. Call it a notebook. He's obliged to keep such a book.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He is obliged because this work notebook is registered, so every company commander, battery commander, is issued with that document, that work notebook. When he fills it out, then he returns it, he is issued with a new one, and he has to copy the basic elements from the earlier notebook.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And his notebook, company commander's notebook will show where he and his company were and in general terms or specific terms what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes, but a company commander for the most part issues orders orally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But as -- the record he keeps -- well, I'll come back to that. You gave an example about somebody, a company commander, going out in a truck and leaving his notebook back at the headquarters. If he did that, he'd still be under an obligation to make daily recordings of what he did when he was away from headquarters, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood the first part of your question correctly, none of my officers took a truck to leave their vehicles behind in headquarters. Their notebooks have to be kept in their bags. And then he writes down everything that he considers important, especially the orders he receives and the orders he issues. Now, it depends from one commander to another. It is not strictly defined what he is going to write down. It is his own judgement. But as a rule, orders received and tasks assigned to subordinate units, that is what he would write down in that notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the question was based on an answer you gave that there were two types of work notebook, and you gave the impression that one of them was a book that the officer would have with him when he was not in his own base, in his own headquarters. Has that been wrongly interpreted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The company commander does not have headquarters. He is always with his troops, and he is the only one who is with his troops round the clock, 24 hours a day. In this notebook of his, the basic notebook, which is registered, he has all basic elements in it, all basic elements that he needs in terms of the life and work of his company or battery. I repeat, he has to have a list of personnel, a list of equipment, who was issued with what, the vehicles that he was issued with, the ammunition. All these basic elements have to be in that notebook. As for the other notebook, through wire communications, wireless communications, courier, he has to record what he received from someone or what he sent out or if he has certain remarks to make when he is touring his troops. A day or two later, for example, he would go and see the same platoon and check with the platoon commander and see whether things were done the way he ordered them to be done. So this other notebook is a personal aide-memoir to him for resolving questions on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What the previous witness, Sel, said at 1324 and 5 seconds - I'm afraid I don't have the page number - of the second day of his evidence, I think, was this, and I'll just read it to you slowly. He said of his notebook -- and he was a company commander: "... all the orders I received orally I entered in there, and later I would receive orders in writing. So in this notebook I would have that -- for example, if I did something wrong, a court of law would only admit the kind of evidence that is contained in a work notebook." Now, that's the transcript. He then went on to say: "That is the regulation -- that's the way regulations are in our country." Does that explanation of his for the significance of notebooks for legal proceedings make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is a question addressed to me, I don't want to make any comments regarding his statement, but documents are not written for courts of law, and that is quite erroneous if Mr. Sel said that. They are written for documentation and to analyse later the combat tasks carried out. And at a higher level it is used for archives or, rather, history that is being written.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None of us would accept to write documents for a court of law. We would not accept that kind of job.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Depending on what he may say about this, it may be that what he's saying is that if by chance you land up in a court, then you require your notebook and the court will -- the courts of Serbia or the former Yugoslavia would require to see evidence in that notebook. I'm only guessing at the moment. Would that make sense to you, that this type of notebook would be generally required by a court if you landed up in a court? Does that seem to be sensible?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably when an important event takes place, when there's some kind of disaster, of course documents are sought that have to do with it , as evidence either for the Prosecution or for the Defence, because it would show whether all measures were taken to protect whatever was at threat and whatever is the subject of the proceedings. But the document itself is not written for a court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I understand that. Thus far, then, we have this picture: For your brigade, there will be three records prepared on a daily basis from the moment that the war started -- the conflict, whatever we describe it, started in March. Three documents -- actually, rather more than three. There will be many -- three types of documents. There will be many company commanders' diaries, there will be several battalion commanders' war diaries, and there will be your war diary, and those documents will give a day-by-day account of the disposition of troops and of what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As a rule, yes. The units keeping these documents enter the most important events on a daily basis, and they inform the superior command of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Moving up from your position as a brigade commander, there will be a Pristina Corps war diary. So that's a fourth tier of record.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, with respect to command. They don't receive war diaries but combat reports. When I get a combat report from a battalion commander, a summary is entered into the war diary and a report is sent to the commander of the Pristina Corps or, rather, to other units at the corps level. And those units also enter the most important events in the units without going into details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assume for the time being, please, that none of these documents has been destroyed by any NATO attack, because that's never been claimed for these documents by the authorities. Assume that, please. The Prosecution in this case has been trying through various means for several years to get hold of the diaries from the battalion level and up, and none has been provided. Is there any reason known to you as a former officer, now retired, is there any reason known to you why those documents should not be made available to a court inquiring into these events?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think there is a single reason why they should not be made available. I'm referring to war documents or any other kind of documents. Unfortunately, most of the documents have been destroyed. I'm not referring to combat documents. I don't want to appear partial, but I will tell you that the families of our officers are still suffering huge problems. They cannot exercise their rights because of the vast amount of documentation that has been destroyed pertaining to their life and work, whether they were members of the army of Yugoslavia, whether they were in the garrison. They cannot solve their housing problems, welfare problems, or any other problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Assuming again, carry on with the assumption that none of these documents has been destroyed in NATO attacks, because that's never been claimed, locating a war diary in a headquarters or archive at the battalion level or above should be an easy matter, shouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If this is kept in a certain place, it's very simple: You find the number and you look it up. However, knowing the actual situation, that the barracks were destroyed, it's impossible for all the documents to be still in existence. Part of the documents, perhaps, have remained behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that now?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because documents are packed into crates. If the command where the documents are kept is hit, it's more than certain that the documents are destroyed. If this was not done, and we see that almost all the commands were hit, then of course the documentation would be complete.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were in the headquarters, were you? Where was your headquarters?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're referring to the command in wartime?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In wartime, my command was constantly on the ground. I spent the least time in the barracks because as of the 25th of March, the command building was hit, and the brigade before that had left. It was in the Urosevac garrison, about two kilometres to the east. And during the war -- shall I explain? During the war, the command divided into several parts to avoid being destroyed, so that if part of the command is destroyed, another part can take over and take command over the whole brigade. The brigade for a while was in the village Doganovic, and it's marked here 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause for a moment. Because I want to save time, but I'm trying to get to the point to help the Court, and I'm sure you want to help us, Mr. Jelic. The Pristina Corps command is the place where these documents would have been sent, and that was not destroyed by bombing and there has been no suggestion that the -- any documents in it were; correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Pristina Corps as a building was not destroyed. However, it was abandoned before the beginning of combat activities. At least seven days before, to the best of my recollection. The entire command pulled out of the building of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I still want you to carry on on the assumption -- I think we've done this now. Just tell us roughly how many battalion war diaries exist to cover this period, assuming they haven't been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a hypothetical question to which I cannot provide an answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how many battalions were there in your brigade? How about that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eighteen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Battalions and divisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we wanted to identify the 18 battalions and divisions by name so that we can make a request, or it may be even an order if the Court is so minded, to produce those documents today, can you please give us the identity of those 18 battalions so that we can be specific in our request.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you have it on the map here, all the commanders of the battalions and artillery battalions, starting from the Armoured Battalion, the Mechanised Battalion, the other Mechanised Battalion, the anti-armour detachment, the Howitzer Artillery Battalion, the Police Battalion, the 252, the -- and so on. These are all the units listed here in the brigade area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can I ask why you spend so much time with witnesses on carrying out Prosecution investigations? Is there not another way of doing this exercise with official channels rather than using all the limited time you have for cross-examination to further the investigation process? Because it doesn't help me in the least, this exercise, I have to say this morning. It's getting nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry about that but in fact it's absolutely essential for the following reason: We've made requests for these documents for years. The Chamber decided that the response of the authorities that the original request was over-broad and burdensome was justified. We narrowed the request down. We got nothing. We reduced it ultimately to a single request for the Pristina war diary. We got nothing. Last week, the Chamber had enormous success in a particular document by an order. Now, the Prosecution's view is that these trials would have been enormously assisted and reduced in length if the original documents that would or should provide contemporaneous accounts had been available. They've all been kept from us, and I'm going to ask this witness some more questions about these documents so far as he is concerned. The only way we can now get them is through the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But since this issue came to light in the evidence of Delic, what discussions have you had with the authorities in Serbia to get these documents which you were then alerted to existed?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've known they've existed. We've tried every method. And since --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not answer I'm looking for. I'm looking for have you been actively discussing with the authorities in Serbia getting these documents, which is a Prosecution task, and you only involve the Court when you fail in your own negotiations to get it. Now, have you been building on what information you got from the likes of Delic and others rather than -- or are you waiting to build some sort of case based on cross-examination of witnesses, which seems to me a method of carrying out inquiries rather than presenting evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly not the latter. We have no interest in spending time in this way if there was any other way of avoiding it. Not only have we gone through all the RFA methods, not only have we tried the 54 bis method, with the success of which -- or limited success of which the Chamber is aware, but there have been direct negotiations at the highest level, leading to promises of the production of documents, all of which have melted away as the traditional snow in spring. And we have got almost nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Be that as it may, Mr. Nice, you must bring this exercise to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, as Your Honour wishes, but can I ask the witness something -- two other questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you'd be good enough, please, Mr. Jelic, to go to any one of these tabs. If you go to tab 12, please, in your documents. Now, tab 12 is just an example. If we look at the top of it, this is a document of yours within a series, and it's confidential 305/2. That may be one series of documents. If we go on to a later period, just have a look at it, go on, please, to tab 19 as an example. Can you go to tab 19, please. We see a document headed 400-336. Do you see that? That's the number at the top.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to 12 or 19 now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm now looking at 19. Number 19. It's strictly confidential, 400-336.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you'd take as another example tab 43. You see there at the top of that page 400-1166. So it would appear to be in the same series of documents but 800 further on. First of all, is it right that there were perhaps two different numbering systems, the second of which begins always with 400, and the earlier system of which begins with different numbers?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did these documents -- who produced, who found these documents that are contained in your file?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the accused and his associates. I see here the numbers that were entered in that period, and at the same time they were registered in the war period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is no suggestion that this selection of documents that we have here from obviously a very wide selection, a very long list of documents, there's no suggestion that any of these documents has been destroyed, any in the, say, 400 series or in the earlier series of documents coming from your brigade. There's no suggestion any of those have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These documents were not in my brigade. They were all outside the brigade because they were handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps. We have not kept any documents in the brigade. According to orders, all documents were handed over to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it would appear - and that's all I need to ask you on this - from the production to you by the accused's associates of these documents that the correspondence files exist and are complete.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. I don't know how they corresponded or from whom they sought the documents or where the documents were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In coming here to give evidence, did you seek to refer to any of the various contemporaneous documents that we've established existed, and probably still exist, other than the particular exhibits that were selected by the associates for you to look at?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not my job to procure documents. The documents shown to me here were documents that I saw and studied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't seek to look at anything else; your war diary, your own notes if you have any other notes. You didn't seek to look at any of that material preparatory to giving evidence?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I didn't want to. I have no right to request documents, to go to archives, to take documents, or to actively look for them. I feel that the documents I received from them are authentic, they're signed, and I conclude that they were copied from the originals and that they are firsthand documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you really didn't even ask to see your own war diary in order to remember what happened?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please bear in mind that I live almost 400 kilometres away from Belgrade. I have neither the time nor the funds to travel to Belgrade and spend days there. I have my family obligations. I cannot enter into an investigation. That's not my job. I have been called as a witness with the documents shown to me. I have been asked whether I wished to testify or not, and I agreed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, reality here is that we've had a lot of military witnesses from various sides, and people with military background, and military witnesses called by the Prosecution for the most part, or if not all of them, have sought to and have referred to contemporaneous notes in order to remind themselves of what happened. Can you explain why it is that you, and if it's a matter of culture that we should understand, other VJ witnesses don't seek to refer to war diaries or notes made contemporaneously. Is there a cultural thing that we should understand, or is there a regulation we should understand?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who used what here or how they presented materials and facts. I'm telling you only about things I know about and only about myself. I studied the materials I was given, and on this basis I came here to testify. I was in no position to obtain documents, to search archives, to look for records, looking for what was destroyed and where. Please don't forget that the corps was moved from its area, that the documentation has been scattered or destroyed, and the documents I received from the accused's associates are the ones that I looked at. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, how long will you be in cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Because you have spend an hour and 20 minutes and you have not yet reached the essentials of this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me make my position quite clear, because it may be that in some way I'm not making it clear. The Prosecution takes the view, which it has advanced in its application for assistance from the Court, that contemporaneous documents should have been provided, and it takes the view that witnesses of this kind who don't seek to rely on them may be witnesses against whom there are observations to be made as to credibility. It seems to the Prosecution arguably incredible people should not, when there are such contemporaneous documents available, seek to refer to them. Whenever we have found these documents, and it is we who have found them in the court process because we haven't been able to get them by other means, they have proved to be of great value to the truth-finding function of this Court. I would respectfully remind the Court of what we discovered from the diaries of Delic, Vukovic, Djosan, and what we're going to discover in due course, and I hope it's tomorrow if not next week. I maintain the position that it is significant and valuable to know that witnesses of this kind make no effort --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But you spend too much time on it. You must move on to the events to which his testimony relates.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You spend far too much time. Let me just say that Mr. Sel, Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Nice and Mr. Kay, will not be testifying this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just on Mr. Sel, I know that Mr. Nice is having passages of his notebook translated, and it would certainly help us if those translations were handed over to us as soon as the Prosecution get them in sections, rather than springing them on us when he is in court and relying on passages that way. We would like to see the translations ourselves in advance, because I know that that's being undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll deal with that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That would be helpful, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that perhaps a little later when I know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice said that witnesses are not making use of contemporaneous documents. All the documents that have been tendered through witnesses - he mentioned General Jelic, General Delic, General Djosan, Colonel Vukovic - all these documents are contemporaneous documents. This claim cannot be made. As for what he says about Djosan's, Vukovic's and Delic's diaries, he found only things that go against what he is saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milosevic. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would press the Court, please, to assist the Prosecution in this problem area by ordering the production of at least four war diaries; the brigade war diary, and the three mechanised battalion -- the three mechanised battalion war diaries, which are likely to be the most valuable ones. The Court's orders made in the course of the trial have so far been respected and swiftly. Any other method - we've tried every - doesn't work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn, then, please, to 1998. Turn to 1998. You went -- or you were in Kosovo in 1998. In the spring of 1998 your function was what, you say?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's a question for me, I said that from 1994 to the 15th of June, 1999, I was the commander of the 243rd Armoured Brigade, which was later the Mechanised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were your duties in Kosovo in 1998, the spring of 1998, for example?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was a brigade commander in 1998, also the commander of the Urosevac garrison.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your brigade doing in the territory? There was no state of emergency. What was it actually engaged in doing?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basic tasks of the brigade. Because it's an old garrison, almost a hundred years old, it's an A brigade, and it was carrying out combat training. That was its basic task. Securing military facilities and the state border.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at a part of this exhibit that wasn't looked at when the accused was exploring it. Tab 3. The first paragraph says this, if you put it on the overhead projector. "The latest operations carried out by units of the Corps in coordinated action with units of the Serbian MUP in curbing terrorism ... were carried out very professionally and responsibly, with sound assessment and prudent use of forces." So first of all, you were actually engaged by August in curbing terrorism, yes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this a proper military activity when there is no declared state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to the rules of service of the army of Yugoslavia, the army can be used for fighting against terrorists and renegade groups. For me, the order of the corps commander is law, and it has to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says this a sentence or so later on -- the following sentence: "An analysis of the achievement of the tasks showed that some units overused combat equipment the consequence of which was greater damage to buildings in areas of combat operations. Specifically, a large number of houses were destroyed and torched." Well, how come, if you were doing the action that you initially told us you were engaged in in 1998, how come your troops were destroying and torching houses?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order of the commander of the Pristina Corps and it pertains to all units in the corps. What is stated here is that there was great damage of buildings in the area of activity. If one bears in mind the way in which anti-terrorist fighting takes place, especially in urban areas, the balance of power has to be 15 to 20 in order to carry out this assignment, and that is according to world standards. That's the ratio. The corps commander will probably carry out an analysis in the corps command, together with his subordinate officers. He came to the conclusion that there was excessive use of force. Perhaps equipment and ammunition were used excessively in order to carry out specific tasks. In order to prevent that from happening, he is issuing an order as to what should be done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Torching -- the word "torched" means, does it not, intentionally setting fire to property? How could it be, please, that units of a Pristina Corps were intentionally setting fire to property in August of 1998?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot see here that there was any intentional torching. I don't know what passage you saw that in. Fires are possible, though. If there is firing in part of a populated area, if there is mutual fighting, often fires break out due to the ammunition used, and at the same time electric installations, and particularly in summertime, can be set on fire and then sometimes haystacks would start burning, too, and that is how buildings were burned. So the -- it doesn't say here that there was torching.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's the way we have it in translation. You better read the sentence that begins, "Specifically, a large number of houses were destroyed ..." Can you read that sentence to us and the interpreters will provide a translation -- interpretation. "Specifically, a large number of houses ..." please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, that is paragraph two?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's at the beginning. It's at the middle of the paragraph. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Most of the objections of the international community came due to the unnecessary --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the wrong sentence, General. It's the sentence -- it's the third sentence in the first paragraph, beginning "Specifically ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "An analysis ..." is that the first word?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "The basis of the reactions of the international community --" is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may be the sentence has been divided in interpretation where not in the original. Can the witness begin the sentence and read through "Analizom ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's practically after the first sentence. "An analysis of the achievement of the tasks showed that some units overused combat equipment the consequence of which was greater damage to buildings in areas of carrying out combat activities." Do you want me to go on? "On the basis of the reactions of the international public opinion, especially intelligence services and diplomatic representatives, most of the objections from the international community came with regard to the unnecessary destruction and burning of houses in inhabited areas, which can jeopardise all efforts being made to crush terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and create conditions for a political resolution of the political crisis in Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'll have to go back and discover, if I can, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But where is the sentence, "Specifically, a large number of houses were destroyed and torched"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- that needs to be explored now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That requires an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I ask one last question about the last passage which I wanted an answer on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and then we have to break.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It ends, as it's translated, that the international community was concerned about the destruction of houses, the destruction and burning of houses, and it goes on to say, "... which can jeopardise all efforts being made to crush terrorism ... and create conditions for a political resolution ..." Do you understand that to mean that the international community would impose a political resolution? Is that what you understand General Pavkovic to mean by that? No, it's "... can jeopardise all efforts being made to crush terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija and create conditions for --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, that's efforts to create conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps I'll leave that and I won't come back to that. I'll investigate this sentence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I asked for the witness to be kept out for just a couple of minutes. With your leave, may we deal with something in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we in public session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should say that logistical problems do not make it possible for Mr. Sel, we understand, to return home and back here for Monday, so he will be here. In that event, Mr. Nice, we would wish to have your cross-examination of this witness terminated - end - today, so that we can conclude Mr. Sel's testimony tomorrow. For that purpose, we may start at 8.00 a.m., but we haven't yet decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. And while the witness is coming in, the interpreters have explained that the document -- the line in the document that was there should not have been there at all. It's an incorporation from another sentence, as it were. So I've struck it through and it simply shouldn't be there at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a very bad mistake. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, in relation to what you mentioned just now, whether it would be possible to start working at 8.00 in the morning, please bear in mind the fact that my floor, which is the last one, is moving to a different building tomorrow, and all my time has been planned in order for me to finish certain things in relation to that before I come here. It's a purely technical matter, and - how should I put this? - it would be highly impractical for me to be deprived of that time for an additional hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take that into consideration, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Nice: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We parted from that last document, Mr. Jelic. The line that we were asking you about is not in the original and has been deleted from the copies. Nevertheless, my suggestion to you is this: That in 1998, you were a loyal officer serving an army that was regularly exceeding what was lawful in the use of violence on the population, and you knew that to be the case.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what you're saying, that I -- well, I was loyal. Of course I was loyal since I made an oath of allegiance to my country and to my people that I would defend my country. Otherwise, I completely reject the other thing you said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You of course were serving in an army to begin with presided over by or led by General Perisic. Were you aware or have you become aware that he complained about the misuse of the army to this accused and was replaced?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of General Staff, General Perisic, toured the units in Kosovo and Metohija several times. It so happened that he visited my brigade three or four times, and he toured the units at Dulje, Stimlje, and Birac. In addition to the military protocol and the obligations I had as the brigade commander and the commander of the garrison, I had no other -- I had no other obligations vis-a-vis him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you answer the question there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to answer the question. I don't know what Mr. Perisic stated before Mr. Milosevic or the Supreme Defence Council or, rather, in that time to the minister of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the answer. The rest of it was immaterial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wesley Clark, the American general, expressed the view that Perisic was replaced because he wasn't supporting the accused's policy of using military force against the population in Kosovo. Is it right that it was effectively this accused's policy in 1998 to use the army against the population? Not just to maintain borders or things of that sort but actually to use the army against population.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what Mr. Clark said. The army had its tasks exactly defined by the rules of service and the laws. So the basic tasks were providing security for the border, training soldiers, and all of that is done in peacetime; and in wartime, defending the country from aggression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at another document, a new document. 8th of August, document, please. This document is a document of yours, 8th of August, 1998. It goes to the command of the Pristina Corps concerning their telegram identified. Perhaps we can put it on the overhead projector. It says this: "In accordance with orders issued, an analysis has been completed of combat operations carried out and cooperation with MUP military units ... The report is as follows:" And then it deals with the combat group in the Dulje pass, gives the strength of those deployed. Over the page, please. At B -- we can read the document for ourselves. Well, there's already reference to the use and deployment of tanks in Dulje, then in Stimlje, C sector, there are seven tanks deployed. Go over to the next page just so that we don't miss the point. Paragraph 3 asserts that: "MUP and VJ members behaved correctly towards civilians and property without abuse of rights or resorting to theft or crime." 4 says: "The units had fair success ... but with the following problems ..." and then complains about the police refusing to take part in attack on a DTG. A DTG being?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabotage terrorist group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that it's clear, isn't it, that the army was engaged in using heavy weaponry on the territory with no state of emergency being declared. Mr. Jelic, that's right, isn't it?
