utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you hear the question, Mr. Jelic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question. This is an assertion. I didn't understand it in the form of a question, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He's asking whether the position is that the army was engaged in using heavy weaponry in the territory in the absence of a state of emergency being declared.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The army used all resources available in order to provide security along the roads. We had orders from the corps command to carry out every one of our tasks and assignments. Not a single assignment was carried out if it was not based on an order. This pertained primarily to roads that were supposed to be cleared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. -- General, the point of the question was whether that was being done without a state of emergency being declared. Just a question of fact. We're not dealing now with the constitutional implications. Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The order can be read for itself. May it be produced as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 933.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The use of the army continued, and we come to Racak, which I must deal with in a limited amount of detail. You gave a lot of evidence about the army and Racak, and the position, I think, is that the army really had nothing to do with Racak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have seen Radosavljevic suggesting that it was a joint -- on an interview with a television programme - we won't rerun it now - we've seen him suggesting that it was a joint operation. Can you explain at all why Radosavljevic should have said that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which Radosavljevic you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The chief of the police who was in charge of the operation, that one, known as Gurij. Do you know who I mean?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Radosavljevic, a major. I am not aware of his interview. I haven't seen that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was subordinated to his own command in Pristina, and he carried out orders of his superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go to tab 8, please. Now, tab 8 precedes, if we look at it, precedes Racak by a few days, about six days. It refers to strictly confidential order, command number 49/1. Have you been shown that document since you've been here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document. The document --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 107-2?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I mean the document that is referred to in the first paragraph. It says: "Pursuant to the strictly confidential order of the Pristina Corps Command no. 49-1 ..." Have you seen that document since you've been here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's here. That was an original document of that time, and on the basis of that document I drew up my own order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because the same paragraph goes on: "... and with a view to ensuring the required level of combat readiness in the forthcoming period, I here by issue the following," and then there's an order. And at number 5 we can see reference to Siptar terrorists. What was the combat readiness that was required of you and why, according to your recollection of that order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order, which was issued by the Pristina Corps command is an order from which this order here followed. Following the rules of issuing orders in the army, apart from the document on which this order is based, all the other elements have to be enumerated. It has to contain all the elements given by the superior command. The focus has to be expressed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Combat readiness for what combat?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat readiness is something that the unit constantly has to have. That's what the army is for. It has to be always ready to respond to any challenge concerning the security of the country, the security of the border, and the protection of the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not specifically related to anything that was going to be happening, say, in Racak in the days to come?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tab 10, please.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see that from the context here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You issued an order on the 15th of January. Again, this is pursuant to, as we can see, a strictly confidential order of the Pristina command number 105-1 of the 15th of January. Have you seen that document since you've been here?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I have not seen that document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Over, then, please -- we're going to start looking --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just check one or two things that you said about Racak itself. You spoke of a blockade, and you spoke of the MUP forming the blockade about 3.00 a.m. and between then and 7.00 a.m.; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information given to me by the chief of the Urosevac MUP and the plan he had in his staff, the MUP units in the early hours of the morning - and the time is mentioned in several places but I wasn't there so I can't tell you what the precise time was - the MUP forces carried out a blockade of the area where Siptar terrorists forces were believed to be before dawn, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army, when you say "blockade," you mean the area designated, which has to be surrounded by designated units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or, I suppose, if not surrounded, certainly blocked in respect of one particular direction of possible escape. Would that be an appropriate use of the word "blockade"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that, but it's not usual to say that. Usually it's when a large area, more than half, is taken by units and then the place is practically under a blockade. The main roads, of course, have to be closed in that case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to have a look at a map that's been used in this trial from time to time. Not a map, an aerial view. While that's being brought in, what was the position so far as your training unit was concerned? You had a training unit, didn't you, engaged at this time in the area of Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's wrong to say that, because we had no units undergoing training in the area of Racak. As I explained last time, the unit was at Dulje, according to the agreement. And that unit held the communication or the road from Stimlje to Birac and carried out training on these axes. Racak is to the side of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at this map on your right-hand side. If the audiovisual booth could focus on it for us, please. It may be -- yes, I think it can. And if it would draw back so we can see all of the map. Where do you say on this aerial view - if you can take just a second to familiarise yourself with it - the army was located? Would the figure A be about right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this place here, if I understand A correctly. The troops were in this area here, in Borovo Suma, or Borovo forest. The upper part of the forest had already been cut down, and this is where the troops were from April until the beginning of the aggression, part of the combat group the command of which was at Dulje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you look, then, to the left of that, B, and the feature running pretty nearly north/south, slightly north-west/south-east. From B, if you look at the bottom of that red area, you will see something that says in English "VJ MUP tank and vehicles." Is it right that there were VJ tanks and vehicles in that area?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was there in this period but there were no troops or tanks there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was the commander of the unit. Of course I knew where my units were on a particular day in a particular period of time. There had to be a plan, an order from the superior command. I had to issue my own order, the subordinate commander of the subordinate units had to issue his command, and only then could a task be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Further south on the map we can see, I think, C on the bottom right-hand corner. May have to move the map across. We see there "VJ/MUP tanks and vehicles." There has been evidence to this effect, that there were tanks and vehicles there. Do you accept the possibility that those tanks and vehicles were there or do you again say that, because you issued the orders, no such tanks?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not because I issued the order but because I did not issue the order that they should be there, so there were no troops there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at those three positions, just for the time being assume that they may be correct: A, the second position marked with tanks and vehicles, then the position C, would that operate as something of a blockade to stop people retreating in an easterly direction?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I cannot assume, because the army was not there. The blockade, as it's shown here, this does not actually show a blockade of a village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The -- tell us, please: The General Staff's operation centre was based where at this time?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly the General Staff's operation centre? I had my corps command, and as for the operations centre of the General Staff, I assume it was in Belgrade. That's where its place was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Orders -- I beg your -- yes. Operations of the kind I'm suggesting happened, that is joint operations between the MUP and the army before the declaration of a state of war, to take out a substantial KLA unit, would such an order have to be -- have to originate in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it had to originate in Belgrade. However, the commander of the strategic rotation group has the right to issue certain decisions about the use of troops at a certain point in order to protect an element of the army combat disposition or part of the territory until the Supreme Council reaches a decision. There was no need in this case because the army was not engaged at all. Only the corps commander could issue an order binding on me, and I could only take measures, and all the subordinate commanders from the lowest level, from company commander to brigade commander, could take measures for the protection of people without orders if they were at threat, but then he would have to immediately inform his superior commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 15th of January? Where were you yourself? You weren't at Racak, so where were you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been in Racak. On the 15th of January, I was in the brigade command in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you know perfectly well, Mr. Jelic, that your brigade was actively engaged in firing rounds into Racak and elsewhere in joint operation with the MUP, and what you're telling us is quite untrue. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know anything about this. I deny it. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did communications pass between the General Staff in Belgrade and your brigade; via Pristina?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to all the rules and instructions about command and control of units, a superior commander commands his subordinate units. In exceptional cases, a second superior can issue a command to a second subordinate, but this is very exceptional and I have hardly ever come across it in my career. I always received issues from -- I always received orders from the Pristina Corps command while I was in the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us that your first -- your -- just to complete that: Communication back up to Belgrade would be via the Pristina Corps in the same way as orders coming down to you would come via the Pristina Corps, yes?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've skipped over a rung in the ladder. Issues from the -- orders from the General Staff had to go to the strategic unit, which is the army. The army issued orders to the corps, and the corps to the subordinate units. The subordinate units issued orders to their subordinate units. So this was the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you described a meeting you had, or an encounter you had, a couple of days before Racak, the purpose of which was simply to inform you, is that right, or for someone to be informed that the Racak exercise was going to happen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what meeting this applies to. You haven't been specific. But if you mean a meeting with the chief of the SUP, then you are right. It's quite normal, when combat operations are being carried out, if my neighbouring units or I are carrying out combat activities, it's normal to inform your neighbouring units. There is reason for that: They have to take precautions, to prevent infiltration of their territory by terrorists. They have to protect their own troops and their own equipment. They have to protect their own area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think you said there has to be the avoidance of friendly fire and the consequences of friendly fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand. What fire are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where troops of the same side accidentally damage each other. If you don't know where they are and you're firing, there's always a risk you'll damage your own side, injure or damage your own side. That's what "friendly fire" means. Was that something that you were concerned about?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't usually call it friendly fire. We use a different term for it. If units are acting together, then they have to establish lines where they don't fire at each other, and if they're acting in built-up areas or so on or where they adjoin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, your only involvement on the 15th, you say, was to fire in another direction and because somebody fired at you. What time of the day on the 15th was that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not only saying it, I'm asserting it. On that day when the MUP units blocked Racak looking for terrorists, fire was opened and the unit that was in the pine wood immediately took up positions. In the meantime, fire was opened on it at around 8.00 or 9.00. It was opened from an elevation that has no name overlooking the village of Belince, some 3 or 400 metres to the south. Not from the village itself but from a nameless elevation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this whole incident was completed by what time of the day?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fire was opened intermittently. Several bursts. Three shells, 82-millimetre mortar shells, and this was confirmed by your witness who was in the brigade. I think his name was Sukrim Bura [sic].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the incident was concluded by what time?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the unit remained in full combat readiness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how was that reported, if at all, to Pristina and upwards in the direction of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the incident that occurred toward the army?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's usual for the commander of the battalion, after taking measures to protect his men and equipment and taking up positions for circular defence according to previously approved plans, after he has taken all these measures and repelled the attack, he then sends a report up the chain of command. That's the chain of reporting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But your report on this incident would not have linked it in any way to the Racak exercise of the MUP, would you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My report could not have had anything to do with the operation because I did not have the information, the elements about what was going on there. I could have known that only if I had participated. In that case, it would have been my duty to report, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Reporting what happened between 8.00 and 10.00 would have contained no reference to Racak because this had nothing to do with Racak.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You always have to give specific information, not general information, about where fire was opened from. You say where fire was opened from, what was done, whether there were any casualties or losses of equipment, vehicles, weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen your report up the chain of command since you've been here, your report on this incident on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the report is here in the file, if I recall. I don't know what tab number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have the -- go -- tell us which one you say is the necessary report. You've started about 12, I think, or 11. Tell us which one you say --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have a look now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's 17, if that's the one you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, it may well be 17 because that does indeed cover these topics. Let's go and look at 17 and see how you expressed yourself then. 17, if we can put it on the overhead projector, please - we must be brief - deals with on the 15th of January the unit from Dulje carrying out regular training, which is why I asked you about training. "While the training programme was in progress along the above-mentioned axis, heavy infantry and RB fire was opened from Rance ... mortar fire from the village ... We fired back ..." No reference to Racak there. "Our forces suffered no consequences." Then this: "In the early hours of the 15th of January, forces of the MUP/Ministry of the Interior/ ... set up a blockade ..." So it was they, the MUP, that set up the blockade. And then over the page, please. 0700 hours, at the top. "... heavy infantry fire opened at MUP forces ... training ..." And then again at the end of this: "MUP forces set up a blockade and searched the village of Racak ..." By the way, the preceding line -- before I come back to the immediate topic, I want you to answer this: Why did you write here: "None of our vehicles entered neither the village of Racak nor any of the surrounding villages"? Why do you think it necessary to put that in your report?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely because fire was opened and returned from our weapons, the corps commander had to know what happened on the ground. That's why I had to report that not a single vehicle from the area entered the village. And this here refers to the village of Racak. Because use of combat vehicles requires that you report exactly where the vehicle went, how far it went, and when it came back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Saying where it did go is different from saying where it didn't go. I'm just wondering why you made a reference in this report to what you didn't do at Racak. Was that because it was a joint operation and you were identifying the limits of your involvement?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no joint operation. If you look at the part here which refers to the opening of fire, it says that the unit returned fire and did not enter the village of Racak. Returning fire is something that's not stationary. These are all highly mobile units, and they respond with fire and assault. They go, take up an area, destroy the target or go on. They're not static, like artillery, linked to one spot so that you have to search for a position for them. That's why this was done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not telling us the truth, Mr. Jelic, as the following document, I'm going to suggest, makes clear.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your conclusion and your opinion. You have the right to it, but I'm telling you how I reported and answered to my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is from the VJ General Staff. It's dated the 16th of January. On the overhead projector. Did daily operation reports get sent down to your level of command? Did they? Did daily --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operations reports of the command of the General Staff. They couldn't have been sent to us. It was we who sent operations reports to our superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, this is their report for the 16th of January, covering the period 6.00 a.m. the 15th to 6.00 a.m. on the 16th. And for want of time, there is no need to go to any part of it apart from, in the English, page 4 and -- I've now mislaid my copy of the original. It's under the heading "3rd Army." Have you found the bit that's headed "3rd Army"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the translation here. Where is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Second page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Second page. I'm grateful to His Honour Judge Kwon. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you find the paragraph immediately before number 9, the cross-heading 3A, for 3rd Army. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you look at the second bullet point of that paragraph, perhaps you would just like to read it out for us from the original to make sure there's no ambiguity in the interpretation or error in the interpretation. Can you just read it out.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be best for me to read out the whole thing so that we'd have the context. That way you can understand it the best. "While a tactical --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My time is limited, but if you want to read the previous paragraph, read that, because it refers to your unit. Yes, by all means. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. "... the 243rd Mechanised Brigade Urosevac in the sector of the Dulje pass near the village of Sefer, Siptar terrorists opened fire with infantry weapons after which they retreated towards the Dara Glava feature. Our forces were unharmed. "Part of the forces of BG-243-1 were deployed to seal off --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read slower if the interpreters are supposed to interpret what he's saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please read more slowly for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... where MUP members were conducting an operation against Siptar terrorists who had killed a MUP member." That is what is written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you read the second paragraph again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Part of the forces of Combat Group 243-1 were deployed to block the village of Racak, Stimlje municipality, where MUP members were conducting an operation against Siptar terrorists who had killed a MUP member."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. Would you like to explain --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is not the original. It's not from the corps or from the army. It does not originate from the corps, from the army, or from the brigade. That's where the unit is. And if it is considered that the unit was there in a blockade, then it was, yes, in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, you've explained how orders of the kind I suggest you were responding to, that is, orders to establish joint operations of this scale would have had to have come from Belgrade. That means they didn't come on the morning. They had to come a day or days before. You explained how the reporting chain went back from you, via Pristina, to Belgrade in respect of, for example, the firing on you of infantry weapons. This document is prepared in Belgrade. If there hadn't -- do you understand this? If there hadn't been a planned deployment to assist the MUP members, then Belgrade would have known about it. How can it be that on the 16th of January Belgrade is recording that part of your forces, number 1 unit, were deployed to seal off -- sorry, to -- to block the village of Racak?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You presented a few different things here, but I have to respond to all. First of all, I personally never received orders from Belgrade. We never got a single document from Belgrade in my brigade. Everything went down the chain of command, through the command of the Pristina Corps. The command of the Pristina Corps has my report, and that report is the only valid one for commanding or, rather, for assessing the situation in the unit. The corps commander is the one who accepts or does not accept the report. It is most probable that the gentleman who dealt with this document - and I don't know who it was who dealt with this document, I cannot recognise the initials - he probably thought that the combat group was already there, as approved by the verifiers, and he said that it was there in the blockade. Now, you look at this. You said yourself a few moments ago that this blockade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pause. As approached -- as approved or something by verifiers. What verifiers say isn't going to be reflected in a record of what your group is doing. What your group is doing is -- in a report like this, reflects what you report. Now, can you explain, please, how what you reported or what has already on ordered comes to be reflected in this way? That's what we want.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The signature on this document is the same like -- or, rather, the description in this document is like what you said by way of a description of this blockade. We saw during the examination yesterday, too, that there is something that represents a blockade for someone, at least as far as movement is concerned, because through the areas of the units, the combat dispositions, that is, you cannot walk about normally like in a free territory where there are no troops, where there is no army, because it would certainly have been stated here in this report had any part of the unit actually been used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must suggest to you that it's as clear as can be that you were engaged in a joint operation authorised in advance from Belgrade, reported back to Belgrade, and that this document proves the lie of what you've been saying.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for the compliment you've just paid me, but that's not true at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this to be exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please give it a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 934.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd just like you to look at this exhibit, already before the Court. You see it relates to the 15th of January between 3.00 and 8.30 in the morning, if you look at the legend at the top left. And it suggests that the 243rd Brigade was present in the position north of Racak, roughly where A is on the overhead view. If you look to the right, right to the east, you'll see another marking, anti-aircraft marking of the army. Was that you there? Just point -- see the place we're pointing to or indicating? Was the army deployed there in the east?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a complete map. I don't know whose map it is, but the PVO system -- the PVO system, the anti-aircraft system -- well, it's not a complete map. So this is not the way you deploy a PVO system. One was at the top of Canovica Brdo - that is here - and one was here by the point, and one was here by Kostanjevo [as interpreted]. Tanks were here and APCs were inside. That is what is contained in the report sent to the corps command. This is a bit distorted. This was after fire was opened at the area of the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, this is a map that's been produced by Janicevic, the chief of the SUP, and he says that you were at least present in two places; up there in the north and there in the east. Is he right or is he wrong? He's a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's quite right, but I've said that the symbols were drawn upside down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So whereas you told us that you were only present in one place, you now accept that you were present in two.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got things a bit confused here. This is a combat group or part of a combat group for Dulje. When fire was opened, units took up positions for defence, and the PVO system was by the point, which is marked here. Then the second unit was above Canovica Brdo; and the third one, Kostanjevo. That is the system of defence. Tanks were not standing in a column. They were to the east of the area of deployment, and APCs were in the middle, and howitzers were on the western side. I'm giving you the details regarding this particular group now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Help me, Mr. Jelic, because I may have missed it. At any time in the evidence you gave yesterday or in the previous day of hearings, did you mention the presence of that unit at Kostanjevo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Kostanje, that's where one Praga was. I don't remember whether I mentioned it yesterday. There was one Praga, the one here, and then one up here, 671 on the top here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked very extensive questions by the Court and by the accused, trying to identify precisely where your troops were located and the short answer is you never mentioned Kostanjevo at all, did you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never even mentioned 671, not only Kostanje. The question was how come the combat group was here and how come the unit that was training was here, towards the village of Rance? If I remember correctly, that's what it was, and you can look it up in the transcript. And whether their command was at Dulje or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look, please, at the board again, the aerial photograph on your right, and at position C. You've denied this morning that there were any troops at position C. It's quite close to Kostanjevo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the unit was not blockade as you had put it. You asked whether these were the units that were engaged in the blockade in those early morning hours, the units that blocked Racak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... go back over the transcript if time allows. You were given every opportunity to say if there were any troops in the Kostanjevo area which you then understood to be the subject of only Prosecution evidence, and you denied it. You're not telling us the truth about what the army did in Racak because you know that the army, along with the MUP, exceeded all conceivable lawful use of force in what turned out to be a dreadful massacre, don't you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true at all. That is what you're saying. Not a single shell, not a single bullet was fired at the village of Racak. And if you look at the map, carry out an analysis and see whether it was possible to engage this equipment that was up here or only perhaps here on the rim of the village of Racak. I think that that was confirmed to you by the chief of SUP, who was, after all, carrying out this action. And there is no need to conceal where we carried out joint operations, because we have documents for that. We have orders from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which war diary or similar contemporaneous document would record the various movements of troops, including, for example, the movement of the troops to Kostanjevo?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A war diary exists only in wartime. This is peacetime. Units are carrying out training in the ground, and that is what I allow for. So there is no war diary for this period. The unit has --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... record will reveal --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the plan of defence. Then there is an order to go out into the field where all tasks are defined; size, numbers, and the tasks of the unit on the ground. It has its plan, and the commander of that group elaborates a plan of defence of a feature, and that plan is strictly confidential, and he defends his unit by taking up new positions outside the camp. That is to say that the unit is not only on the camp premises. Once it is attacked, its equipment and personnel take up positions and defend their units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, we do have an operations log that has been provided for your unit or the relevant unit. I can make it available to you, perhaps over the break. There seems to be no reference of any kind to what happened on the 15th of January. Could you explain that? We'll let you have a look at it. How could the operations log not make reference to these events on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just guess now, because I don't see anything in front of me, I don't have the documents, and I don't know what you're talking about at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have a look at this document which has been provided to us, and you can tell us what it amounts to because it's one of your documents. Perhaps we can just lay this on the overhead projector and you can follow, if you would be so good, the original handwritten entries, which we hope are correctly translated. That is a combat group for Dulje Heights, as we can see on the left, commanded by Lieutenant Colonel Dragan Todorovic. Is that about right for the unit you've been describing in the single position in which you've said there were troops?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I'm not mistaken, that's from that period. But it's not very well written, so I'd really have to have a look to see what this is all about. I cannot really comment on it straight away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll take you, for your consideration, item 1 deals with something that happened on the 14th of January. Then item 2 simply says that the composition -- disposition of the unit is unchanged. It deals with Frasna and Boja. It deals with Birac. It deals with the consumption of fuel. Nothing else. And then the next day is the 16th of January. Any explanation how this isn't covered at all in this document?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to have a look first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the witness have the opportunity to look --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- at it over the break, if he wants to, to save time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not encouraging the Court to break now because I would be very grateful for the opportunity of asking one more question for preparatory purposes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we distribute this map again now, please. Different topic but I'm trying to save time. Place it on the overhead projector, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is another updated version of the document we were looking at earlier which you helped us with. Now, in giving evidence yesterday, you spoke on no occasion of being present at any particular alleged crime site on the occasion of any particular alleged crime. You only ever told us what you'd been told. This map attempts to analyse, so far as is possible - and again, this may not be a final version so I only want you to use it for reference purposes at the moment - it attempts to analyse the material before this Trial Chamber concerning alleged VJ criminal behaviour between 1998 and the end of 1999, with dates. I'm not suggesting it's an exhaustive document, but it's doing its best to guide us through a great deal of material. Would you please look at this document and tell us if you were in fact personally present at any of the events on the dates referred to so that, for example - I know sometimes the dates are not precise - the first one, top left-hand corner, says that something happened at Jezerce in September 1998 and also in 1999. We can see what it is a bit later if we have time. But then going around, Belince on the 4th of April. Racak, we know you weren't there. Stimlje three dates. Muhadzer Babus, two dates in March. Urosevac, dates in March and April. I want your help, please, Mr. Jelic - and it may be again that the Chamber will allow you to take this document with you to save time - I want you to tell us, either now or after a break, whether you were present at any of these places on the times indicated. Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your two questions. First you said that these were crime scenes, and then you asked me whether I was there at the time. So, practically, you are giving ambiguous questions. You are stating that a crime was committed somewhere where people are fighting with arms in their hands and where young men who swore an oath of allegiance to defend their country are getting killed, and you are trying to rehabilitate those who got killed as terrorists in order to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You misunderstood the question. I'll make it clear.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- our crime.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are places where various crimes or criminal behaviour is said to have been committed by the VJ. It's your area of responsibility. And so far as possible, dates or precise dates have been given. You, yesterday, on no occasion asserted that you were present at any of the scenes that the accused referred to where crimes were said to have been committed on the material dates. Can you please look at these various entries and tell us, perhaps after the break, whether indeed you were. Let's have a look, for example, at the one that was covered. Slatina, middle of the map, 13th of April, 13th to 15th of April. Were you ever present at Slatina between the 13th and the 15th of April, 1999? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. That's a very brief period of time. It's just one day or two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. That may apply, then, for Vata and Dubrava. What about Bicevac on the 25th of May? Were you present there in May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in that area for over a month, in this total area. But in the village itself, I was never there. I've already said that the command post of the brigade was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I will allow the witness to take the document with him during the break and have a look at it, and then equip yourself, if you can, to answer questions. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there was reference at the beginning of this session to the order of the 31st of October, which I've now had an opportunity to read. It's a clear prescription of how to obtain documents. It was never -- it doesn't at any stage involve a denial, an outright denial of any part of the Prosecution's application.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to this, I just wish to make an objection, in relation to this question that was put to the witness, telling him to have a look at during the break. Mr. Nice is putting questions to the witness as if he were a tourist and whether he happened to be somewhere. This is a commander of a brigade who is testifying about what happened in his area of responsibility. He is present in the entire area of responsibility throughout his units, and he cannot be questioned as if he happened to be an accidental passerby, whether happened to be somewhere or not on a particular day. He is there 24 hours a day, and General Jelic has already said that he never left his area of responsibility and that he was with his troops on the ground all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see the difficulty. The document identifies a number of alleged crime sites, and the question is fairly simple. The witness will look at the document, and if he can, he is to say whether he was present. If he doesn't remember, he can say so. So let us adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The daily operations log that you looked at, which makes no reference to any event on the 15th of January of the kind you've described, can you now explain, please, if at all, why not?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written by the commander of the combat group who was up there, and his report for the most part corresponds to the report provided in tab 17, which I have before me and which I put forward here two days ago. This lists mainly the combat activities on two axes; those of Luznica and Rance, and there is nothing here about combat operations being carried out. The commander of the combat group probably was of this opinion. He was the one who had to decide what was to be included at any given point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you do see the problem, don't you? Here's the man preparing his daily report who should have set out all the detail about Dulje because he was there. Nothing in his record. You were at Urosevac. You would have a daily record of the same kind. We've applied for that and it's been denied us or simply has never been provided to us despite specific requests for it, so we have no idea what appears in your daily record. And Belgrade records that you were engaged in effectively a joint operation with the MUP, but also records the firing to and from Rance. It's impossible, on the material provided, to understand why this man's record is so woefully incomplete.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have made certain claims here, and you've twisted the word order a little bit. In the Belgrade report, it never says that we participated but that the unit was allegedly in a blockade in the area where it was. The commander of this combat group had the right to make a personal judgement as to what he was to enter into the diary. In my report to the corps command, in tab 17, there is a detailed description of what went on during those two days, the 14th and the 15th. That's in tab 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I quite understand that tab 17 is a long time later -- not a long time later. It's the 17th of January, two days later. It's not the contemporaneous record that we're looking for. Now, in Urosevac police station, if that's where you were, your daily record would set out what you were receiving by way of information and what you were send on, presumably, to your superiors, and we don't have it, and we don't know what you wrote.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I would be in the police station and ask them for reports. I didn't give them our daily reports, nor did they give me their daily reports. In the police station in Urosevac and Stimlje in this period, I didn't go there. I neither received reports from them nor sent them reports. There was no reason. Had we been carrying out a joint operation, we would have had a Joint Command post, we would have commanded the units jointly and written joint reports, each to our own superior command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't mean to say Urosevac police station, your headquarters there, there should be the record of your communication with the Urosevac police, or with anybody else, setting out what you did. That's what I intended to say. Sorry about that. How were you able to right tab 17, then, if you didn't have information from the police, if we look at it, if you weren't in communication with the police? It sets out clearly what the police apparently claimed to do. Where did you get that from?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first information I said we had a meeting at the invitation of the chief of the MUP, Bogoljub Janicevic, in Urosevac. On that day they were to carry out an anti-terrorist action in the broader area of the village of Racak. I saw their plan concerning that action. In the plan, the army of Yugoslavia was nowhere mentioned, nor was there any written order for the army of Yugoslavia to be involved. I only received information from him as to what they would be doing there. In view of the fact that what was planned was carried out for the most part, on the basis of this I compiled a report about events in the area of responsibility of the whole brigade, and especially in the immediate vicinity of my unit. There are no details here as to what the MUP was doing or anything concerning the events in the village because I had no elements and no need to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at your own document. You set out what they did, not what they planned to do. You say that they set up a blockade. You say that they returned to base at 1600 hours. Of course you were in contact with the police. You couldn't provide that information otherwise.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the exchange of information, but only in exchange of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, can this daily record be produced as an exhibit, not in a sense because it's particularly valuable, it may become valuable later, but because in our efforts to provide a complete file of Racak materials this is the best we've been provided with so far by the authorities because, as I explained, the record of this particular witness has not been provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jelic, very rapidly, where were you on the 16th of January?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 935.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you on the 16th of January, please?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, as far as I can recall, I was in the corps command, attending a meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The corps command in?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Pristina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you knew, then, did you, that Maisonneuve tried to make contact with you and spoke instead to Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that he was trying to have an interview with me. He established contact with Petrovic and talked to him. That's what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And we know -- if we can lay tab 28 of the Racak documents on the file -- on the overhead projector - thank you very much - which is Exhibit 178. I gather I'm failing to identify existing exhibits by number often enough for the assistance of those who properly require it, and I apologise for that. You see, you haven't brought with you, have you, any record of this meeting, the meeting on the 4th of February? This is in English, I'm afraid. Have you brought with you your own record of the 4th of February?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just have a look now. I haven't brought any documents nor do I have any documents. I have no private archive anywhere, but I do have the documents I was given here, if this is it. I'll just have a look.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not there unless you've got more documents in your file than I have. And did you keep a record of your encounter with Maisonneuve on the 4th of February; and, if so, where is it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole meeting with him was held in the garrison command, and it was chaired by the liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you keep a record of it? Where's your record?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted the main points in the document I had with me, and that is a notebook which was later handed over to the command, along with all the other documents. The corps command, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, can I just take you to the second page - please, Mr. Prendergast - so that we can see if you agree with the record that has been made by those who did make the record which is available to us. Your notebook isn't. You appear as J. I'm sorry it's only in English because I suspect you can't necessarily follow that. And is it right that Maisonneuve explained in your presence that Petrovic had explained the role of the army to him on the earlier occasion?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall what Petrovic told him before that at the meeting. We had a joint meeting, the two of us, with him, and I can't remember the details because a lot of time has elapsed and I don't have the documents with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You confirmed, if we look at the second page, that you were responsible for the whole region. You said that the commander of the operation was a professional soldier and every soldier gets his orders and acts accordingly. You went on to say: "The main thing, the VJ did not conduct this operation but were in a position to defend themselves from their own position." Did you say that to Mr. Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. I cannot remember the details but every professional soldier is responsible for his unit. I was responsible for the entire area of responsibility where my units were. If I understood you correctly, that was the essence of your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go on to say, when asked if the village had been surrounded, that the military defended its position. "If you were in Racak, you could see that the hills and mountains with trees are not good for tanks." And did you then later say that you weren't attacked from the village but from the high ground between Racak and Belince? "This was not a military operation, nor were the VJ responsible for any destruction in the town. Our operation happened at the same time as the MUP operation." Did you say those things to Mr. Maisonneuve?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We partially agree here. The army had no plan and no orders to block the village of Racak. Look at the mountains here. You can't actually see it here, but if you have a map on a smaller scale you will see what the hills were like, and the mountains. In view of the configuration of the terrain, tanks and combat vehicles cannot reach the point overlooking the village of Racak. It's impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must suggest to you that by the time of this meeting where Maisonneuve explained how Petrovic had been embarrassed as a result of what had happened, didn't on the note set out what he had said specifically but said that he was embarrassed, I must suggest that by the time of this meeting there was already a plan and you were acting in accordance with that plan to try and eliminate the VJ from Racak because you knew what a terrible event it had been, and that guides both what you wrote in your memorandum, in your document at tab 17, and what you said to Maisonneuve when he managed to reach you. Is that the truth?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the truth. There was no plan, either from the superior command or the corps command. That is, there was no document issued by me or my subordinates. The only document I saw the day before was at the Ministry of the Interior, that is with the chief of the SUP in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. No, something else. I'll move on. Oh, yes. His Honour Judge Bonomy, I gather -- I understand last week was raising, maybe with you or with another witness, I think with you, the question of a report by the VJ into Racak. Now, has there been such an inquiry or such a report, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the part of the army, no report was sent to the corps command. There was no investigation, because there was no reason where the army was concerned. The investigation was by the MUP. They recruited a lady, I can't recall her name right now, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... concerned, then apart from the document we've looked at and has been produced by an exhibit coming from the General Staff, is it your evidence that there is unlikely to be any other document coming from the army analysing what happened at Racak on the 15th of January?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no document investigating that part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- either in connection with officers or civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to this document that we've produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's an aide-memoire. You'll see -- it's an aid. You will see it's the same format as the document produced for Delic. Of course it isn't evidence in itself. It identifies where evidence may be found and it may that the Chamber will find both documents helpful, and I'd ask therefore that consideration be given to marking it as an exhibit on that basis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, have you been able to look at this map; and if so, are you now able to tell us whether you have firsthand knowledge of any of these identified scenes of alleged crimes? Firsthand knowledge; you there?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is not a village in which the unit was deployed that I did not visit more than once. I told you where the brigade command was, and I spent days and days there, especially in Bogdanovic and Djeneral Jankovic, where the focus of the defence was. If I put this map over my map where the decisions are, it's almost identical, and this confirms what I have been saying over the past few days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you understand my question or not? Is there any of these --

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question fully. You probably expect a different kind of reply from me. These are units where my units were attacked, where allegedly innocent civilians were killed, only don't forget that these civilians were armed. Nobody's asking about the soldiers who were killed. Twenty-four soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause, Mr. Jelic. You haven't answered my question. You've answered another one. Let's go back to my question. Is there any instance drawn from this map where you are in a position to give us firsthand evidence, because you were there, of what happened? Take any one of them. Sojevo, north-east, 8th of April, 1999. Were you in Sojevo on the 8th of April, 1999? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall the date. I can't recall the exact dates on which I visited various places. I had this plan, but I don't have it any more. I don't know when I visited which unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you see, the next thing is the answer you gave me was this, you said: "These are units where my units were attacked, where innocent civilians were killed -- where allegedly innocent civilians were killed ..." but don't forget the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that looking at all these points that we've identified here, you recall that these are all places where your units were attacked?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are mostly places where units were attacked by two brigades of terrorists which were in the areas of Kacanik and Stimlje, and another one was later established. In the brigade, that's where there were the most casualties, especially on the road leading from Doganovici towards Globocica and Brezovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So you now remember these places as scenes of attacks but you have no contemporaneous document with you of any kind that can tell us what was reported to you of what happened; is that right? There is no contemporaneous document with you of any kind?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have those documents and those reports. Yesterday, in a part of the tab shown here, I listed the names of soldiers from these combat groups who were killed, from privates to lieutenant colonels. We had enormous casualties. These casualties did not occur by accident. These were attacks by terrorists on military vehicles and the positions of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, then, I'm going to deal very briefly with the crime sites because you simply can't help us with any detail. But before I come to that, my general suggestion to you and one further exhibit. The truth is that from the launch of events in the middle of March, there was a campaign to move people out of areas and to be prepared to kill them when those operations were happening. Right or wrong?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that is unknown to me and the army, and it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we look at your tab 19, just to refresh our memories, this is the only order that you've produced -- not only order, but this is an order that you've produced for this particular day, the 26th of March, and the previous document that we've been shown is dated -- undated. Undated, the previous one, but in any case, this is the 26th of March. And if we look at it very rapidly, this is to do with the enemy who is identified in three ways under the bullet points as NATO, then as Albanian terrorists, then again as Albanian terrorists from Kosovo and Metohija. So this focuses on NATO but it deals with Albanian terrorists, or alleged terrorists or whatever. It sets out what the various decisions are and what you've got to do. And you told us yesterday about your functions at this time, which were what, to deal with the border principally at this time?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me add to your comment. It's not "alleged terrorists," but they really were terrorists. Every country in Europe and in America called them terrorists up to about six months ago. Later, when they organised them, they called them the KLA. I cannot respond if the question does not correspond to the truth. I cannot talk about alleged terrorists but only about terrorists, because that's what they were, and the entire world was calling them that. If we want to analyse this order, I cannot skip over certain things and answer only questions about some bullet points. I have to go into a detailed analysis. We have five brigades on a border where there are terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: General, just answer the question that is asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer a question that is pulled out of context because then I have no response. In order to give a response, I have to explain what this is about and then base my answer on that. So I would like to explain this in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you understand the question to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three kinds of terrorists or enemy are being asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You weren't asked that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I misunderstood the question. Could it be repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put the question again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your evidence yesterday this document admittedly identifying three parts of the enemy; NATO, SDS and STS, this document, you told us, says what you were to do; is that correct? I know it's your order but it sets out what you were told to do.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do we have the order coming to you from higher command of which this is a reflection?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that order with me, nor is it here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you now please look at this document, which is dated the 24th of March, two days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court wants to make a decision about exhibiting the aid, dealing with the aid as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It appears to partake more of an internal aid, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm entirely -- it's a matter for the Chamber's convenience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the order that I've now handed to you is dated two days earlier. It comes from something called the Joint Command. Just tell us what the Joint Command was.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking to see if I received this order. I don't see that it has anything to do with this order of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if you'd go, please, to paragraph 5.4, which is on English page 6, it clearly has to do with your brigade.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The combat group of my brigade is referred to here, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to the last page, you'll see it's signed by the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That's what it says, the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is one document that has been provided by the authorities. First of all, you were the man receiving this order, what was the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw the Joint Command nor do I know who was at its head. If this did exist, it existed at a higher level, but I would have to know, when I receive an order, who signed it. Like any order, all orders I received were signed by the corps commander. So the brigade is used exclusively by the commands of units. Possibly this is a plan that was made in coordination with somebody else from the system of the armed struggle or, rather, units of the army of Yugoslavia in order to carry out coordination with all units. In principle and in actual fact the commands of brigades, or at least I'm talking about myself, I only had orders from the corps commander registered, and that is how I had them registered, uncertain numbers. I don't know about this command because I didn't participate in it. I am a tactical unit, a joint tactical unit and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go to paragraph 5.4, and while you're going back to that, let me just inform you that your brother brigade officer, Delic, accepted receiving a broadly -- a broadly similar order relating to his unit. It's tab 356 of the Delic exhibits, with which the Chamber will be familiar. I provide with you that piece of information. Now, look at 5.4. "The 243rd Mechanised Brigade is to be brought in from the deployment sector on the 25th of March to the planned sector in Lapusnik and from the seal-off line of Orlate village - Belince village - Mlecane village, supporting MUP forces in the attack. "Task: Support MUP forces in defeating and destroying the STS on the axes of ..." and then it gives several villages: Mlecane, Murga, Donje Obrinje, Orlate, and so on, "... and destroy the STS in the sector of Plocica." Now, it goes on: "Continue the attack, destroy any straggling parts of the STS on the attack axes ... Use some of the forces to seal off the line ..." Understand, Mr. Jelic, this has been provided to us as a legitimate order existing, of the Joint Command, on the 24th of March, 1999. Did you receive those instructions?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot recall whether I received this order. As for the Joint Command, I repeat: I never participated in it, nor do I know who was on it and who made the decisions in this Joint Command. I claim that all orders for using units were issued to me by the corps commander. Nobody else but him. Now, again I'm saying that it's possible there was some coordination involved here as to what should be done and that was derived from that was an order, either on the basis of a telegram or as an order. I'm not sure because I didn't participate in this and I cannot make any comments and it would be unfair vis-a-vis the document, vis-a-vis the people who were there, if they were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Jelic, amongst the various contemporaneous documents that existed and probably still exist, there will be one recording the receipt of written orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. All documents that come in have to be registered and signed by appropriate individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Next, you say you don't know if you received this order. Did you in fact receive orders in some way so that the description of what you're to do here matches what you did?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically it relates to this example, and I cannot remember, in view of the time, whether it corresponds or not or whether it was in that area or not. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at it. "Support MUP forces in defeating and destroying the STS ..." That's what you were engaged in as from the 24th of March, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. Not every day, but where communications were threatened, where accessibility was threatened, and where units of the sabotage terrorist groups were, in breaking them up, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it appears you did receive an order somehow in line with that. And you were there to defeat and destroy the STS, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for every activity to support the MUP forces, there had to be an order, written traces, a telegram at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Here's an order, and coming in the way it does from the authorities, the reasonable inference is it went to you, and you can't deny it because we haven't got the contemporaneous documents. You acted in accordance with what's instructed here, didn't you, and when you -- let me just finish it. And when you produce to tab 19, which we didn't have time and don't have time to go through in detail, suggesting that you were much more engaged in perhaps looking at NATO and in guarding the border, matters of that sort, you're actually misleading us, and that's what I'm suggesting to you, Mr. Jelic, because this order shows the truth. From the 24th onwards, you were unequivocally in joint operations with the MUP to destroy the STS.

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your conclusion is completely wrong. The 24th of March is D-Day for the army of Yugoslavia. You know how the decision was made, and before that, with our units, for the most part we took up defence regions. This is only the final part of the document that I issued and that we got from the corps commander. That is to say, taking up the borders in order to have a blocking defence of the state territory. I think that it is sufficient evidence that on the map it says where the map comes from and what the source is. So it is approved, the Pristina Corps, excerpt from my brigade. So there is no reference to some Joint Command on this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, on this document, which I'd ask to be exhibited in a minute, here you are in charge of a brigade. Who did you understand to be your political masters once a state of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Political leaders for my brigade? Primarily for me? Were the decisions of -- and the decision of the Assembly. No political leaders or political parties. You know, if you looked at our rules, that in the military, in the army, it is professional soldiers and civilian soldiers employed in the army are actually banned from being members of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Armies at war respond to civilian leaderships unless they are in -- under martial law. Who was the civilian authority giving instructions to you, the brigade commanders, through Pristina Corps and other higher authorities? Who was the civilian leadership that you understood?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No civilian leadership issued orders or decisions. It was the Supreme Defence Council or, rather, the Assembly that declared a state of war. I personally did not contact anyone. It's not that somebody came to me and gave me instructions or support or told me in any way what I was supposed to do during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May this become exhibited, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am saying that I don't understand what document Mr. Nice wants to have admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Joint Command document produced by the authorities pursuant to a request and apparently relating to this witness's brigade and in respect of which it appears he acknowledges acting in some conformity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Has its authenticity been established?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, documents coming from the authorities are typically regarded as what they appear to be. We can see one other way in which I can verify it -- not verify, but at least ask about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you are not objecting to this, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. I think this document was admitted while General Delic was giving evidence, and I tendered it. I think it's the same document. Or maybe it isn't. Maybe it's just similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's similar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. In any event, we'll admit it and we'll have it checked out as to whether it was already admitted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Jelic, if you go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's have the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 936.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you go to your tab 19, paragraph 5.1, English page 3, in a document that may focus on other topics such as NATO, we nevertheless do find a reference to crushing and destroying the STS. We can see it in the first part of that. It says: "In the current deployment sector be on standby ..." and so on for various things, and: "... destroying the STS along the following axes: Dulje village, Belanica village, and Semetiste-Kravoserija, by separate order ..." Now, what do you understand by "separate order"?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you understand what a separate order is? So if an order is issued, then this is an order as to what the battalion commander is supposed to do. He took up positions in the Dulje pass and he was given a task. It has to be carried through, just like when anti-aircraft defence is concerned. That is to say that if forces move against him, he should attack those forces and destroy them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm interested in your observations on is this: Is the order I've just presented to you and that has now been exhibited an example of the separate order dealing with destruction of the STS, even though you may now say you don't remember it? Isn't this an example of that separate type of order?

utterances.speaker: KRSMAN JELIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. First of all, this order that you showed me just now does not pertain to my order, the order I issued, at all. Not in terms of its content, not in terms of the tasks involved. So that's a document that you brought in here from the Joint Command. This is a combat order pertaining to this map on the basis of the decision of the corps commander or, rather, my decision and my order. The order is complete if it is on a map and if the text is written out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Court was aware yesterday that I wasn't going to pass on all the documents I indicated of things to raise.
